commit-quiz
A
pre-commit
hook that verifies the developer
actually read their changes
before committing. Useful when AI agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex…) generate
the code and the dev just hits "commit" without reviewing.
Every AI code-review tool reviews the code. This one quizzes
you
.
npm install -g commit-quiz
commit-quiz install
#
in the repo you want guarded
How it works
On commit, the hook takes the staged diff (
git diff --cached
).
It sends it to an AI CLI you already have and generates
4 statements about
the diff: 2 true and 2 plausible-but-false
(wrong file, inverted
condition, different value…).
The dev marks which ones are true:
In a terminal
: interactive prompt, with colors.
From the editor UI
(VS Code, Cursor — no terminal): native dialogs
(macOS via
osascript
, Linux via
zenity
when installed), including a
"generating…" heads-up and a verdict dialog with the real summary when
the answer is wrong.
On a correct answer the commit goes through. On a wrong one the commit is
aborted and the
real summary
of the diff is shown.
The hook is
fail-open
: if the LLM does not respond, there is no network, or
there is no way to ask, the commit goes through with a notice. A gate that gets
in the way ends up disabled; this one only gets in the way when it can do its
job.
Privacy
What is sent?
The staged diff (
git diff --cached
, unified context of 1
line), truncated to 30 KB, plus a fixed instruction prompt. The diff carries
the paths of the changed files in its headers, as any diff does. Nothing else:
no repo name, no git history, no author identity, no other files.
To whom?
Only to the AI provider you already use, through its own CLI and
under your own account:
claude
→ Anthropic,
codex
→ OpenAI,
gemini
→
Google. The diff goes from your machine to that provider's API, the same path
it takes when you use the CLI directly. There is no commit-quiz server, no
shared key and no middleman. Which provider is used is yours to pin with
git config commit-quiz.cli
.
When?
Only on commits with 20 or more changed lines (configurable), and
never on merges, rebases or cherry-picks. Everything below the threshold is
never sent anywhere.
What does commit-quiz keep?
Nothing. There is
zero telemetry
. The
optional debug log (off by default) records timings, the chosen channel and
your answers, never the diff.
What is excluded by default?
Lockfiles (
pnpm-lock.yaml
,
package-lock.json
,
yarn.lock
,
Gemfile.lock
,
Podfile.lock

*.snap

*.svg

Add git pathspecs, per repo or
--global

git config --add commit-quiz.exclude
"
config/credentials/**

git config --add commit-quiz.exclude
"
*.pem
"
git config --add commit-quiz.exclude
"
db/seeds/customers.rb
"
Excluded files are not sent and do not count toward the line threshold.
How do I skip it for one commit?
COMMIT_QUIZ=0 git commit …
(or
--no-verify

Not yet. Providers are a small table in
src/providers.js

few lines, and contributions are welcome.

How does it work?
Instead of storing your files as bytes, lgit trains a small neural network to memorize them. Each commit is a training run: the network learns to map positional encodings to your data, byte by byte for code or pixel by pixel for images. Checkout is inference: the network reconstructs what it can from its weights
The network uses Fourier positional encoding, ReLU hidden layers, and an Adam optimizer. For text, it outputs a probability distribution over 256 byte values. For images, it predicts RGB values directly. A small network compresses aggressively and hallucinates. A larger one memorizes perfectly but defeats the point
And it all runs in your browser

Where the expert weights live

cache of its own: the macOS file cache

the missing ones are read from the SSD in parallel. The answer never depends on
this: if a page is still missing, the GPU simply waits for it.

Verify routes experts on the GPU.
Each layer's router also guesses the
next layer's experts for every row. Those guesses (for layer 0, every expert
already in memory) go to the GPU with the layer, and a planning kernel picks
out the ones the rows actually chose. The CPU only runs the rare route
that wasn't guessed or whose expert is still on disk. It plans the same
routes as the CPU would; the tests check this end to end, by comparing
speculative output with plain decoding.
The drafter's inputs never pass through the CPU.
The main model copies
the six hidden-state layers the drafter reads into a ring buffer on the GPU,
as part of each layer's work.
One wait per step.
Behind each verify, on the GPU, the drafter adds the
verified tokens to its context, compares its drafts with the main model's
choices, moves to the main model's next token and drafts the next block. The
next verify reads that block straight from the drafter's buffer.

The drafter's 4-bit weights are installed
once into a file and read in place, like the experts.
Sampling keeps the speedup.
With a temperature above 0, every token is
drawn the same way everywhere: the largest of (logit ÷ T + noise), over the

token's position and the token (the Gumbel-max trick, an exact sample from
the tempered distribution). The drafter draws its guesses with the same
noise, so a draft is kept exactly when it equals the main model's own draw.

same text plain decoding draws, and on the benchmark prompts sampling at
temperature 0.6–1.0 ran 1.4–1.9× faster with the drafter, as greedy does.

where two tokens score almost equally: verifying several tokens at once does
the arithmetic in a different order, which can flip a near-tie. In greedy
testing the first such difference came after 90 to 356 tokens; with sampling
it is a near-tie in the noisy race, as rare (one of twelve 192-token sampled
runs differed, from token 32).

With only one link, every single spike ends up right on your face.
So the Frame can do two links, but my PC only has one WiFi card. And I don't own another WiFi 6E card... or so I thought. Turns out laptops have WiFi too. So I grabbed my MacBook and used it as a hotspot while it was connected to my network over Ethernet. In typical Apple fashion this was not as straightforward and very buggy to set up. However once it worked, I had a new AP which I could even move and that was not stuck to an antenna somewhere under my desk.
The "Adapter"
As you might have guessed by now, the MacBook hotspot situation again has only one radio and I had no adapter. So I needed to use the same mechanism as the Adapter to connect my PC's WiFi card to the Frame somehow. At that time I did indeed not know that it is just a hidden hotspot from the Frame side. I searched every settings menu to see if I can change where the second radio connects to, but found nothing.
Luckily the Frame is just Linux. Linux machines normally have terminals. Terminals normally don't hide their secrets. Secrets normally are just a command away.
To make my job even easier, Valve actually gives an option to enable SSH on the Frame.
Once I connected to the Frame via SSH, I found out that
softapmanager
is used and it opened a hidden network called
frame_XXXXXXXX
plus a 32 character password. It uses the separate
wlanap
interface.
On my PC I just connected to that network and it worked... ish?
Multilink Streaming
Streaming via Multilink (so over both radios) worked! But is my motherboard WiFi card now an official Valve adapter? Depends on who you ask.
The Frame has two different places that show the adapter. The first one says Valve's adapter is not connected. Fair enough, it isn't. But once you actually connect and look at the other one, it proudly tells you that you're connected via WiFi and Valve's own adapter!
So the Frame disagrees with itself. And SteamVR? SteamVR said the adapter was connected the whole time. If even the Frame is confused, I don't feel too bad about being confused either.
A Small SteamVR Rant (Feel Free To Skip)
Quick detour before the interesting part. SteamVR on Linux is... an experience.
Connecting, even without my Frankenstein setup, was a pain. Sometimes it took a minute to connect. And every time I pressed the connect button while waiting? Saved up and replayed afterwards. All of them. Great experience!
I've also seen a number of interesting crashes in both SteamVR and Half-Life: Alyx. No idea if that's the Frame or just Linux being Linux. One of them I traced down to a poisoned mutex in Alyx, which then spawned an SDL window, blocking, on the main thread. So the game looked frozen or crashed while it was really just waiting on that window.
Okay, rant over. Back to the WiFi.
Okay, this is nice, but how does it work?
So far I knew three things: the Frame has a hidden hotspot, it runs on its own
wlanap
interface, and the Adapter is just a WiFi 6E dongle. What I didn't know: how does Steam know the credentials for that hotspot?
My goal was simple: A tool which connects your PC to the Frame's hidden hotspot, without the Adapter and without SSH. And oh, I am unsure if I would do it again...
Getting the credentials was easy if the Adapter had been connected once, since Steam stores them in a NetworkManager profile. But I wanted them without ever having connected the Adapter.
This is the part where my understanding of how it works changed multiple times!
Down The steamclient.so Rabbit Hole
So I found a really cursed way to get them. The credentials usually get shared via Steam's local Remote Play protocol, and the thing speaking that protocol on your PC is
steamclient.so
. So the plan was: load
steamclient.so
into my own program, connect to the running Steam and just ask it nicely.
Here is how "just ask it nicely" went:
Load
steamclient.so
, call
CreateInterface
, connect to the running Steam over its IPC pipe. So far so good!
Find the methods I need, like
PairViaWifiAP
. They exist! They're just not exported. They live in private C++ interfaces nobody is supposed to touch.
No exports, so I go through the vtable. Object pointer, table of function pointers, pick the right slot, call it and hope.
To find the right functions, read the ELF at runtime and look for the instructions that load the method's name. Then hash every function I call, so I don't accidentally call something else.
Steam updates. 15 of 16 hashes change.
PairViaWifiAP
moves from slot 55 to slot 61.
Add an option to ignore the hashes. Basically a "trust me bro" flag.
Steam beta: "Steam has no
GetRemoteClientCount
". It does! The compiler just loaded the string into
R13
first and then moved it to
RCX
, and my scanner only looked for
RCX
.
Write an actual instruction decoder that follows registers around. In theory it now recognizes every Steam version I could find, going back a year. In theory....
It was a real mess and some of the worst code I have ever written, but it worked. I was able to get the credentials from Steam directly without having the adapter connected!
Works On My Machine
Well, the only problem was that the other machine was also mine.
On my second PC, which never had the Adapter connected, it just didn't work. So I spent a lot of time debugging different
steamclient.so
versions, only to realize that my mental model was fully wrong.
My mental model: the Frame owns the password, and Steam asks for it. So I just had to find the asking part.
Reality: Steam on my second PC never got the credentials. It never even tried. And my main PC? It just handed me cached credentials from the last time the real Adapter was paired. So my "it works!" was actually "it remembers!".
The Clue
Looking back, two error messages should have tipped me off way earlier.
The first time I talked the Remote Play protocol myself, I got: "unauthorized". Fair. Just being on the same LAN doesn't mean you get to mess with someone's hotspot. You need to be paired.
Much later I came back with proper authentication and asked again. This time it didn't say "unauthorized". It said: "No dongle present."
Not "here is your password". Not "go away". "No dongle present." As if the dongle had to bring something to the table... Oh fuck wait!?
Reverse Flow For Credentials
Turns out that neither the Frame nor the adapter is responsible for setting up the credentials. It is Steam itself. Steam derives an SSID and password using information from the adapter and sends them to the Frame via the Remote Play protocol. The Frame then sets up its hotspot with those credentials.
So all I had to do was the same thing Steam does, just without the adapter. By default the tool generates a random SSID and password, but you can also pick your own and use your creativity!
Interestingly enough, this works the exact opposite way of how the Frame WiFi works itself. The Frame opens the AP and the adapter connects to it. Normally the access point picks the credentials and the clients join. Here, the PC decides, and the Frame, the actual AP, just hosts whatever it's told.
How It Works Now
All that cursed
steamclient.so
code? Gone. Deleted. Never to be seen again, I hated it anyways.
Instead, it just speaks the Remote Play LAN protocol itself:
Find the Frame on your normal LAN, the same way Steam does.
Connect using the keys Steam already saved when you paired your PC with the Frame. So yes, you still need to pair them in Steam once.
Tell the Frame "yes, I totally have a dongle". There is literally a
wifi_dongle_present
flag for that.
Hand it an SSID and password.
Wait for the Frame to confirm it actually took them.
After that, NetworkManager connects your WiFi card to the Frame's new hotspot. No dongle, no SSH, no reading assembly at runtime.
Want To Try It?
You need:
Linux with NetworkManager
A WiFi card that can do 6GHz and WPA3, and a regulatory domain that allows it. The Frame's hotspot used 6GHz, 160MHz and WPA3-SAE in my setup, so an old 2.4GHz card won't cut it.
Steam running with Remote Play enabled, as the same user that runs the tool
Your PC already paired with the Frame in Steam
The Frame awake and on the same LAN as your PC
Rust, OpenSSL 3 development libraries and
pkg-config
to build it (or just download it from actions)
cargo build --release
./target/release/steamframe-link devices
#
Generate credentials, send them to the Frame, and save them locally.
./target/release/steamframe-link set-creds
#
Connect your WiFi card using the saved credentials.
./target/release/steamframe-link setup --iface wlan0
Want to pick your own SSID and password? Get creative:
./target/release/steamframe-link set-creds --ssid frame_MYPC --psk-stdin
Heads up:
set-creds
changes the Frame's hotspot and can interrupt its current wireless connection.
The profile on your PC doesn't become your default route, so your normal internet keeps working while you're connected to the Frame.
All the other options
Passwords
must be 8 to 63 printable ASCII characters, SSIDs 1 to 32 bytes without control characters.
--psk PASSWORD
works too, but puts the password in your shell history.
Saved credentials
live in
$XDG_STATE_HOME/steamframe-link/CLIENT_ID.json
(default
~/.local/state/steamframe-link/
). They're saved
before
sending, so a dropped connection can't lose a generated password. Retry them with
set-creds --saved
, show them with
set-creds --saved --reveal
.
Confirmation:
the tool only treats credentials as set when the Frame answers with success or reports the matching network hash. A disconnect or timeout is never success, and
setup
refuses unconfirmed credentials.
Several Frames:
use the ID from
devices
with
--client ID
. (If you really have multiply, why not send one to me? 🫣)
Discovery blocked?
Use
--host FRAME_LAN_IPV4
.
--steam-dir PATH
picks another Steam install,
--timeout SECONDS
sets the provisioning deadline (default 30s).
All in one:
setup --provision --iface wlan0
provisions the Frame and sets up your PC.
Already know the credentials?
setup --iface wlan0 --ssid NAME --psk-stdin
doesn't touch the Frame.
setup --from-nm
copies Steam's existing NetworkManager profile.
Plain
setup
doesn't need Steam running or LAN discovery.
--no-connect
saves the PC profile without activating it,
--no-autoconnect
disables autoconnect.
Without
--iface
, the tool auto-detects Valve's adapter. The profile uses WPA3-SAE with required management frame protection, hidden SSID probing, no power saving and the radio's permanent MAC.
--wpa2
is there for compatible setups.
Manage the PC profile with
up --iface wlan0
,
down --iface wlan0
and
remove
.
So, Was It Worth It?
Was it faster than just picking up the Adapter from where I left it? No. Not even close.
But I now know more about the Steam Frame, the Remote Play protocol and
steamclient.so
than I ever wanted to. And you can now (hopefully) use your own 6GHz or 7GHz  (⁶🤷⁷) WiFi card as your "Adapter".
If you made it this far, consider smashing that ⭐ at the top of this page. It costs you nothing and makes me very happy. And when a Steam update inevitably breaks something, you know where the issues tab is.

A live map you can rewind, that tells you where every contact came from.
There is no shortage of dashboards that draw aircraft and ships on a globe.

self-hosted and keyless like those, and then does the two things they don't.
It keeps history you own.
Flightradar24 gates replay at 7 days free,

A devbox task or app that asks for `gpu="AppleSilicon"` now runs natively on your Mac, so `torch.device("mps")` and MLX work the way `"cuda"` does on a cluster.
The Flyte devbox is where I iterate on ML code before it goes anywhere near a cluster: `flyte start devbox`, write a task, run it, look at it in the console. On an Apple Silicon Mac there's been one glaring gap. The devbox runs every task and app in a container, and on a Mac that container is a Linux VM. Linux has no Metal, so `torch.backends.mps.is_available()` is `False` in there, MLX doesn't run at all, and the 40-core GPU on my laptop sits idle while my training loop crawls along on the CPU.
So we added an Apple Silicon accelerator to the devbox. You ask for it the way you'd ask for an A100:
Copied to clipboard!
env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(
name="apple-silicon-train",
image=flyte.Image.from_debian_base().with_pip_packages("torch", "torchvision"),
resources=flyte.Resources(cpu=2, memory="4Gi", gpu="AppleSilicon"),
)
and start the devbox with one flag:
Copied to clipboard!
flyte start devbox --apple-silicon
That's the whole API. `gpu=flyte.APPLE_SILICON()` is the same request if you prefer the device helpers (`flyte.GPU`, `flyte.TPU`, `flyte.AMD_GPU`).
What actually runs where
The obvious design is to pass the GPU through to the container. That isn't possible: there's no Metal inside a Linux VM to pass anything to. An earlier version of this work kept the task in its container and gave it a host-side MLX model server to call over HTTP. That's useful if all you want is completions, but it means your code can't touch the GPU itself. You can't move a PyTorch model to `mps`, you can't train, and you can't load an arbitrary Hugging Face model.
So the default is the other way around.
The workload's code runs natively on the Mac
, and the container becomes its proxy:
The container starts as usual. Its Flyte entrypoint (`a0` for tasks, `fserve` for apps) sees that the backend scheduled it as an Apple Silicon workload and hands its own invocation to a bridge that `flyte start devbox --apple-silicon` runs on the host.
The bridge builds a cached `uv` environment for macOS from the image's pip packages, rewrites the in-cluster endpoints to the devbox ports the Mac can reach, and runs the same entrypoint there.
The container streams the host process's log, mirrors its exit code, forwards aborts, and for apps forwards its port, so the console, the run's logs and the app URL behave as they would for any other workload.
From the console's perspective, a task ran in a pod and produced outputs. From the Mac's perspective, a Python process ran in `~/.flyte/apple-silicon/envs/...` with the GPU right there.
On the backend side, a pod that requests the `APPLE_SILICON` device class gets no GPU resource request (no device plugin could satisfy it, so it would sit `Pending` forever) and no GPU node affinity. Instead it gets the bridge's endpoint and a per-workload HMAC token, so one workload can't talk to another's process.

...

Proving it's the GPU
"It feels faster" isn't evidence, so the SDK ships a proof task (`examples/accelerators/apple_silicon_proof/`) that fails unless five checks pass. Because the code runs on the Mac, it can gather the evidence itself:
Where it ran:
`platform` reports `Darwin arm64`, not the container's Linux.
What GPU:
MLX reports an Apple M5 Max (`applegpu_g17s`), 40 GPU cores.
PyTorch on mps:
a 4096×4096 fp32 matmul ran at 13.4 TFLOPS on `mps` vs 1.6 on the CPU.
MLX on the GPU:
36.5 TFLOPS on the GPU device vs 1.6 on the CPU.
What macOS saw:
the IORegistry's `Device Utilization %` (the counter Activity Monitor's GPU History draws) averaged 93.5–94.7% during the GPU work vs 30% at idle.
The same checks run as an app, behind `GET /proof`. The runbook next to it also covers checks that don't trust our code at all: watching Activity Monitor, reading the IORegistry counter in a loop, and finding the `a0` process with `ps`.
The tradeoffs
Running workload code natively on your Mac means running it
outside any sandbox
. That's the price of real GPU access, and it's why `--apple-silicon` is opt-in. When you pass it, the devbox publishes every port on `127.0.0.1` only, so nothing else on your network can submit a workload that ends up running on your laptop. If you resume a paused Apple Silicon devbox, its bridge comes back without the flag; if the existing devbox was published on every interface, it refuses and tells you to recreate it. That keeps the network out, not software already on your Mac: the devbox API is unauthenticated, as any local dev server's tends to be, so treat an Apple Silicon devbox like one that can run code (because it can).
The rest of the sharp edges:
No silent CPU fallback.
Ask for `gpu="AppleSilicon"` on a devbox without the flag, an Intel Mac, Linux, or any real cluster, and the task fails before it starts with `APPLE_SILICON_NOT_AVAILABLE` and a message naming why. This is deliberate. A training job that quietly runs on the CPU is worse than one that fails.
Only pip packages carry over.
The Mac's environment is built from the image's pip packages, not the image itself, so apt packages and anything else baked into the image aren't there, and neither are k8s-mounted secrets.
It's the devbox, not a cluster.
The accelerator is never cluster-schedulable, and a single workload can't claim more than the Mac's one GPU (`AppleSilicon:2` is rejected).
Several at once share one GPU.
Each Apple Silicon workload is its own process on the Mac, so a fan-out works: `examples/accelerators/apple_silicon_fanout.py` ran eight training shards concurrently. They time-share the GPU, though. A job that already keeps the GPU busy gained little (1.0–1.35x aggregate throughput at 2–8 shards), while a small-batch job that left it idle much of the time gained 1.3–2x. Memory is the real ceiling: every process loads its own torch, Metal context and model.
"mps" on the devbox, "cuda" on a cluster.
The program doesn't move between them unchanged: you change the resource request and the device string. Everything around them stays the same: inputs, outputs, caching, logs and app URLs all go through the devbox exactly as they do on a cluster.

Security
Post-quantum hybrid key exchange prevents future quantum computers from decrypting recorded traffic. Forward secrecy via periodic re-keying limits exposure if a session key is ever compromised.
By default, identity persists across sessions (so saved contacts keep working), encrypted with a per-install master key stored in the OS keychain (macOS Keychain Services, Linux Secret Service, Windows Credential Manager). Headless setups fall back to
~/.config/keibidrop/.master.key
(mode 0600). A passphrase (Argon2id) can protect it for users who back up the config to a cloud. Incognito mode uses a new key pair for each session and writes nothing to disk, so two sessions cannot be linked.
